newsitem.title: MACAU: Portuguese leader visits China, confident in Macau.
newsitem.headline: Portuguese leader visits China, confident in Macau.

text.p: Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio travelled to China on Sunday after visiting Macau where he predicted a smooth transition of the tiny Portuguese-administered territory to Chinese rule.
Sampaio left for an eight-day stay in China after paying his first official visit to Macau.

His China trip was meant to generate "a new political impetus" in Sino-Portuguese relations, particularly over Macau's transitional issues, and to improve business ties between Portugal and China, he told a news conference on Saturday.
There "exists no problem that cannot be resolved in this transition process" ahead of Macau's reversion to China on December 20, 1999, he said.

All the enclave's transitional problems, including those on citizens' rights, liberties and legal guarantees, could be resolved before the return based on "respect for the Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration", he said.
The Joint Declaration, signed by the two countries in 1987, governs Macau's reversion.

Liberties and legal gurantees for Macau residents beyond 1999, and continued Portuguese nationality for the territory's Portuguese passport holders after the handover, would be on the agenda of his talks in Beijing, he said.

About 110,000 of Macau's 455,000 residents hold Portuguese passports. While Lisbon has pledged all the passports will remain fully vaild beyond 1999, Beijing has said ethnic Macau Chinese can use the papers only as travel documents.
China does not recognise dual nationality while Portugal does.
Sampaio, the third Portuguese president to visit China, is due to meet Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng.
His 180-member delegation to China includes Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama, Macau Governor General Vasco Rocha Vieira, and Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho.
Beijing and Lisbon have described their relations over Macau as "excellent".

Macau's coming reversion to China brings to an end nearly 450 years of Portuguese administration. Like its neighbour, Hong Kong, which reverts to Chinese rule at midnight next June 30, tiny Macau will become a Special Administrative Region of China.
Sampaio added that he was confident the local administration was able to fight crime.
"We have to fight all that is negative, we have to fight the things that disturb the transition period," he said.
Macau has been hit by a string of violent crimes since late 1995, including 14 attacks with home-made bombs.
Police say they believe most of the bombings were "acts of revenge" by rival organised crime gangs, called triads.
